items.title: AMD and Meta Advance Strategic Partnership to Power Meta’s Superintelligence Infrastructure
items.content:
AMD and Meta Advance Strategic Partnership to Power Meta’s Superintelligence Infrastructure :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD and Meta Advance Strategic Partnership to Power Meta’s Superintelligence Infrastructure
October 27, 2026 9:20 am EDT
Download as PDF
News Highlights
AMD and Meta collaborate across CPUs, GPUs, networking, systems and software to power Meta services and AI infrastructure
AMD Helios rackscale solutions will power Meta’s leading frontier models and services
AMD technology is the compute engine of choice for Muse and AMD technologies provide Day-0 support for leading Meta models
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct.  27, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today highlighted its deep strategic partnership with Meta, announcing AMD Helios™ rackscale solutions are running at Meta, AMD EPYC™ processors power Meta’s Muse AI agent, and AMD technologies provide Day-0 support for Meta models including Muse Spark Open and Muse Glimmer.
This builds on years of co-design and collaboration between the two companies across AMD EPYC™ processors, AMD Instinct™ GPUs, AMD Pensando™ networking and AMD ROCm™ AI infrastructure.
“Meta is a strategic partner for AMD, and we have built this partnership through years of deep technical collaboration – from EPYC processors powering Meta’s infrastructure to Instinct GPUs and open software supporting its AI workloads,” said Lisa Su, Chair and CEO, AMD. “With Helios now running at Meta, we are taking that partnership to a new scale in the superintelligence era. Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta’s most ambitious superintelligence models and services.”
“AMD has been a key partner in building out the compute that's running our frontier models,” said Mark Zuckerberg, founder and CEO, Meta, “We're making big investments in the computing power that will enable us to bring personal superintelligence to everyone, and AMD plays an important role in that.”
AMD Powering Meta Infrastructure, Today
AMD technology powers Meta’s infrastructure across compute, networking, systems and software.
Initial AMD Helios rackscale solutions are installed and being tested by Meta on the path to a broader deployment in the near future.
AMD EPYC processors support the dedicated computing environments behind Meta’s Muse personal AI agent. Meta has deployed millions of EPYC processors across multiple generations and is a lead customer for 6th Gen EPYC™ CPUs. The companies are also collaborating on future generations, including “Verano.”
AMD Instinct GPUs are currently used in production in Meta’s infrastructure for training, ranking and recommendation engines. Meta was also an early definition customer for the AMD Instinct™ MI450 architecture, and it will deploy a custom AMD Instinct GPU that is optimized for its workloads. The collaboration is also informing future AMD platforms, including AMD Instinct™ MI500 series GPUs and next-generation rack-scale systems.
AMD and Meta have worked together to advance ROCm through PyTorch to ensure that developers can leverage AMD GPUs right out of the box. As well, AMD delivered Day-0 support for Meta's Muse Spark Open models on AMD Instinct GPUs and for Muse Glimmer on AMD Ryzen™ AI PCs and AMD Radeon™ GPUs.
AMD and Meta have
expanded their software collaboration
to large-scale AI training, optimizing recommendation models on AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs and contributing improvements to PyTorch, Triton and ROCm for other developers to use.
As Meta grows its AI capabilities, the companies are working together across silicon, software and systems to address the demands of operating AI infrastructure for billions of people. The companies have aligned product roadmaps and engineering decisions around current and future Meta workloads, evolving years of collaboration into building and deploying integrated AI systems at gigawatt scale.
In addition, AMD will invest $1 billion in Meta’s equity offering.

Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
View more
Anthropic’s
life sciences team
is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines:
BigHat Biosciences
,
Bristol Myers Squibb
,
Divergence Labs
,
Enveda
,
Generate Biomedicines
, and
The Column Group
. We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here
.
There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like
proposing initial designs
for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.
Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.
So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.
This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.
In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.
Case studies
Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering.
Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer.
Read more
, and see
Generate’s technical report
.
Divergence Labs: hit generation.
Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms.
Read more
, and see
Divergence’s technical report
.
BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization.
BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly.
Read more
, and see
BigHat’s technical report
.
Enveda: manufacturing and filings.
To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error.
Read more
, and see
Enveda’s technical report
.
The Column Group (TCG): company creation.
Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs.
Read more
.
More recently, we’ve also begun working with
Bristol Myers Squibb
(BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.
“We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.”
Michael Pourdehnad, MD
, Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy.
In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028.

and see
our technical report
.
Extending our work in the life sciences
All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly
preclinical—
that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage.
This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out
Claude Science
, our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing
Claude credits for life scientists
. We’ve also created the
Life Sciences Verification Program
to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an
open call for guest investigators
in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas.
We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below.

BF16x9
on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs accelerates large GEMMs in the Point Edge Transformer by 2.2–2.5x for a 17,280-atom system and 1.2–1.4x for a 192-atom system, with error below the model’s own non-determinism.
TF32x3
on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs speeds up major GEMMs by 1.7–1.9x and the full molecular dynamics step by up to 1.5x while keeping force error near the FP32 baseline.
TF32x3 preserves potential-energy smoothness and energy conservation in NVE trajectories, matching FP32 behavior where one-pass TF32 shows drift and roughness.
In structural relaxation of a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab, TF32x3 converges in 218–222 steps with a 1.5x per-step speedup, while one-pass TF32 fails to reach the force tolerance even after 1,000 steps.

Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Atomistic simulations help researchers understand how molecules and materials behave, from chemical reactions and phase transitions to mechanical failure. These simulations come with a cost-accuracy trade-off. Quantum-mechanical methods such as density functional theory (DFT) can provide accurate energies and forces, but their computational cost often limits their use for large systems or long simulations. Classical interatomic potentials are much faster, but their fixed functional forms limit accuracy and generalizability across different atomic environments. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) help bridge this gap. They use neural networks to predict potential energies and interatomic forces at a fraction of the cost, enabling researchers to study larger systems and longer timescales while retaining much of the required accuracy.
Running an MLIP efficiently, however, presents its own challenge. Atomistic simulations are sensitive to small errors that can accumulate over time and are most visible when computing forces, which are obtained by differentiating the predicted energy. During molecular dynamics simulations, these forces guide updates to atomic velocities and positions over many timesteps, making numerical precision important not only for physical accuracy but also for the stability of the resulting trajectory.
For this reason, many MLIPs continue to run inference in FP32, even though modern NVIDIA GPUs offer substantially higher matrix-multiplication throughput through low-precision Tensor Core operations. Tensor Core methods for FP32 matrix multiplication offer a way to narrow that gap. They decompose each FP32 operand into lower-precision components, evaluate their cross-products on Tensor Cores, and recombine the results in FP32. This approach can increase matrix-multiplication throughput while retaining accuracy close to native FP32, without retraining or changing the model’s weights or architecture.
In this post, we evaluate how Tensor Core FP32 methods perform in practice on the Point Edge Transformer (PET), a transformer-based MLIP developed by Lab COSMO at EPFL. PET spends much of its runtime in highly optimized general matrix multiplications (GEMMs), leaving limited headroom for further optimization and making it a demanding test case of whether these methods can deliver additional performance gains.
We evaluate BF16x9 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and TF32x3 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, comparing kernel and end-to-end molecular dynamics performance and trajectory-level behavior. We further test the TF32x3 method for potential-energy smoothness, energy conservation, and structural relaxation. We show how these methods can accelerate MLIP inference while retaining behavior close to the FP32 baseline and outline how to evaluate them on other precision-sensitive scientific machine learning workloads.
How Tensor Core FP32 closes the hardware gap
Modern NVIDIA GPUs deliver substantially higher Tensor Core throughput for BF16 and TF32 than for FP32 matrix multiplication, creating a gap between the available throughput at lower precision and the precision requirements of many scientific workloads. Tensor Core FP32 methods help narrow this gap by decomposing FP32 operands into lower-precision components, evaluating selected products on Tensor Cores, and recombining them with FP32 accumulation. Depending on the method and workload, this can deliver accuracy at or near native FP32 while taking advantage of higher Tensor Core throughput.
Figure 1. The BF16x9 algorithm on Blackwell GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into three scaled BF16 components, producing nine pairwise products that are accumulated in FP32 along five anti-diagonal bands
On Blackwell GPUs, NVIDIA cuBLAS provides a
BF16x9 Tensor Core path
(Figure 1). Each FP32 operand is decomposed into three BF16 components, and nine pairwise products are recombined with the required scaling. cuBLAS can enable this path through the
CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1
environment variable, so compatible PyTorch GEMMs can use it without changing the model architecture or implementing a custom GEMM.
Because this approach changes how GEMMs are evaluated, it may provide additional gains when combined with optimized graph construction, fused operations, custom kernels, and NVIDIA CUDA graphs. We did not measure the combined gain in this evaluation; it should be established end to end for each workload.
Figure 2. The TF32x3 algorithm on Ampere GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into a leading TF32 component and a smaller residual component. The leading-by-leading and two leading-by-residual products are accumulated in FP32; the residual-by-residual product is omitted
The
TF32x3
method
applies the same principle on Ampere GPUs (Figure 2). TF32x3 represents each FP32 operand using a leading TF32 component and a residual TF32 component. Unlike BF16x9, our TF32x3 implementation does not use scaling factors. It evaluates three cross-products and omits the residual-by-residual term, as shown in the following equation

NVIDIA CUTLASS provides this approach through the

operator. Inputs and outputs remain in FP32. Tensor Cores execute the three TF32 products with accumulation in FP32.
Benchmarking Tensor Core FP32 matrix math on PET
We evaluated the 26M-parameter PET-MAD small checkpoint (
pet-mad-s-v1.6.0-nn-32
) on a 192-atom water box and a 17,280-atom supercell. We also evaluated the 255M-parameter large checkpoint (
pet-mad-m-v1.6.0
) on the 192-atom system. We compared predicted energies, forces, and stresses with those from the native FP32 path.
BF16x9 method on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs
On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with compute capability 10.0 or 10.3, cuBLAS supports enabling BF16x9 through an environment variable, math mode, or compute type (requested with
CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_EMULATED_16BFX9
,
CUBLAS_FP32_EMULATED_BF16X9_MATH
, or
CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1
). No model-code changes are required to use this path for single-precision general matrix multiplication (SGEMM).
Figure 3. With BF16x9 Tensor Core math for SGEMMs, large GEMMs in the PET model were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload and 1.2–1.4x for the 192-atom workload
Figure 4. MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager BF16x9 modes, relative to compiled FP32, on a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell
With BF16x9 on Blackwell, large GEMMs in PET were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload (Figure 3). Figure 4 compares MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager strategies against compiled FP32.
192-atom system:
The performant strategy sped up the MD step by 1.2x, while the eager strategy achieved 1.1x.
17,280-atom system:
The performant strategy achieved a 1.7x speedup, while the eager strategy achieved 1.4x.
The performant strategy uses BF16x9 when cuBLAS expects it to be faster; the eager strategy uses it whenever the operation supports it. Importantly, the error due to the BF16x9 Tensor Core method is below the model’s own level of non-determinism. This result is significant because PET already expresses much of its runtime as optimized GEMM work, and yet the BF16x9 path exposed performance headroom without retraining the model, changing its transformer architecture, or writing custom kernels.
TF32x3 method on Ampere GPUs
On Ampere GPUs, we implemented TF32x3 by replacing PET’s standard
nn.Linear
layers with a custom
TF32Linear
layer that calls a CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel.
CUTLASS C++ provides a reference implementation of this approach in
Example 27
. The key setting in the PET implementation is:
C++
cutlass::arch::OpMultiplyAddFastF32
This selects CUTLASS’s fast, accurate FP32 multiplication mode. The kernel represents each FP32 operand as leading and residual TF32 components. Tensor Cores then evaluate three products—leading-by-leading and the two leading-by-residual products—and accumulate them in FP32. The smallest residual-by-residual product is omitted. The CUTLASS C++ operator is declared with
float
inputs and outputs. PET therefore continues to supply ordinary FP32 activations and weights and receives an FP32 result; from the rest of the model’s perspective, the layer behaves like a standard
nn.Linear
. Only the implementation of the underlying matrix multiplication changes. The C++ example is written for
sm80
(Ampere) and can also be compiled for
sm90
(Hopper).
The custom
TF32Linear
module replaces compatible PyTorch linear layers and performs their matrix multiplications using the CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel while preserving the trained weights, bias, and input shape.
Because PET calculates forces by differentiating predicted energies, TF32x3 is also used to propagate gradients to the layer inputs. This ensures that both energy and force calculations use TF32x3 Tensor Core arithmetic. Weight gradients use the standard PyTorch path, but they are not required during fixed-weight inference.
Figure 5. TF32x3 Tensor Core math accelerates large PET SGEMMs on an NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU by 1.7–1.9x relative to native FP32 for the 17,280-atom workload
Figure 6. MD-step speedup and single-point accuracy for one-pass TF32 and TF32x3, each measured against its own FP32 baseline
Across PET’s major linear-layer shapes on A100, TF32x3 accelerated GEMMs by approximately 1.7–1.9x (Figure 5). Figure 6 compares MD-step speedup and single-point accuracy for one-pass TF32 and TF32x3, each measured against its corresponding FP32 baseline. One-pass TF32 achieved higher speedups, but at a greater cost to accuracy and trajectory stability (Figures 6–7).
Small checkpoint (26M parameters):
Results are shown for a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell. TF32x3 kept the force error to roughly three times the difference between FP32 runs after recompilation and sped up the MD step by 1.5x on the larger system.
Large checkpoint (255M parameters):
On the 192-atom system, TF32x3 achieved a 1.4x speedup, compared with 1.2x for the small checkpoint. Its force error was 3.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV/Å, essentially unchanged from the small checkpoint.
Validating physical consistency
For molecular simulation, matching isolated energy and force predictions is only the first test of numerical fidelity. Forces are gradients of the learned potential-energy surface and are integrated over many timesteps, so even small numerical irregularities can roughen the surface, destabilize trajectories, or produce unphysical energy drift. The promise of the Tensor Core FP32 method is therefore especially compelling: it can unlock Tensor Core performance for matrix multiplications while preserving the smooth and stable behavior expected from FP32.
We tested potential-energy smoothness and energy conservation using two separate tests (Figure 7). To test energy smoothness, we dragged a single CO molecule rigidly away from an on-top site of a Pt(111) slab and evaluated the total energy at 60 carbon heights from 1.2 to 6.0 Å in steps of 8.1 × 10⁻² Å. TF32x3 followed the smooth FP32 CO/Pt(111) energy curve, while one-pass TF32 introduced visible point-to-point variations.
In a separate NVE simulation of a 192-atom water box, FP32 and TF32x3 showed comparable bounded energy fluctuations, while one-pass TF32 showed a larger systematic drift. These results show that TF32x3 preserved potential-energy smoothness and maintained energy conservation in the tested systems, not just single-point accuracy.
Figure 7. CO/Pt(111) potential-energy curve and total-energy drift during a 30 ps NVE trajectory of a 192-atom water box
Testing structural relaxation
Structural relaxation also tests numerical fidelity as the optimizer repeatedly uses predicted forces to update the atomic geometry. Small force inconsistencies can alter the optimization path, increase the number of steps required, or prevent the system from reaching the desired force tolerance. We relaxed a 539-atom
Cantor-alloy
slab using PET and the FIRE2 optimizer with the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit. Across three replicates, FP32 converged in 218 steps and TF32x3 in 218–222 steps; every run reached the 1.0 × 10⁻³ eV/Å force tolerance. With one-pass TF32, all three replicates failed to converge within the 500-step limit, and forces plateaued around 1.2 × 10⁻³ eV/Å.
TF32x3 accelerated each optimization step by 1.5x while matching the FP32 convergence rate and criterion (Figure 8). One-pass TF32 achieved a 2.0x per-step speedup but failed to converge even after doubling the optimization step limit to 1,000 steps.
These results highlight the practical value of the Tensor Core path: substantial acceleration without sacrificing the convergence behavior of the FP32 workflow.
Figure 8. Per-step speedup and force convergence for FP32, TF32x3, and one-pass TF32 across three replicates of a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab (Co₁₀₈Cr₁₀₈Fe₁₀₈Mn₁₀₇Ni₁₀₈) relaxed using PET and the FIRE2 optimizer in NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit
Limitations and decision criteria
End-to-end gains depend on system size and the share of runtime spent in GEMMs. Small systems generally benefit less because launch overhead, neighbor processing, graph operations, and other non-GEMM work make up a larger portion of the runtime. Larger systems benefit more when GEMMs account for more of the work. TF32x3’s performance also depends on kernel tuning for the model’s matrix shapes and hardware.
Numerical behavior depends on the Tensor Core strategy used. In matrix-multiplication tests,
BF16x9 matched or exceeded native FP32 accuracy
against an FP64 reference, supporting its use as a drop-in replacement for FP32 GEMMs on supported hardware. TF32x3 has a slightly different accuracy profile and should be validated against the model’s accuracy and physical-stability requirements.
Conclusion
Tensor Core FP32 methods improved PET performance without retraining or changing the model architecture. TF32x3 accelerated major GEMMs on A100 by up to 1.9x and the complete molecular dynamics step by up to 1.5x. BF16x9 accelerated major GEMMs on an NVIDIA B300 Tensor Core GPU by up to 2.5x and the complete step by up to 1.7x. As demonstrated for TF32x3, Tensor Core methods preserve behavior close to FP32 in the tested energy-conservation and structural-relaxation workflows.
These results support evaluating the methods in other MLIPs and precision-sensitive scientific machine learning models whose runtime is dominated by large FP32 GEMMs. Neither of the Tensor Core FP32 strategies requires retraining or an architectural redesign. Each can therefore be evaluated as an independent performance layer and combined with other software optimizations when the workload supports it.
Try TF32x3 or BF16x9 Tensor Core methods with your model today—no retraining or architectural changes needed. Learn more in the
cuBLAS documentation
and the
NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit documentation
. Explore the PET models in the
UPET repository
.

Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4
Using the open-source GPU Fractioning Operator and KAI Scheduler to enforce per-workload memory limits at scale
Oct 27, 2026
By
Ekin Karabulut
,
David Lifshitz
and
Hagay Sharon
Like

AI-Generated Summary
GPU Fractioning Operator
is a new open-source Kubernetes operator hosted under the KAI Scheduler organization on GitHub.
It runs alongside the
NVIDIA GPU Operator
to set up and supervise Multi-Process Service (MPS) on every GPU node, apply per-workload memory limits and compute modes, and measure memory and compute use per GPU fraction rather than per whole GPU.
CUDA 13.4 introduces a memory boundary enforcement that is transparent to applications, offering exact memory amounts, guaranteed minimums with burstable maximums, and a choice between time-slicing and sm-sharing compute modes.
KAI Scheduler v0.18.0 integrates with GPU Fractioning through its NvFractions GPU-sharing mode, writing per-container Pod annotations that specify memory requests, limits, compute mode, and GPU device assignments for the operator to enforce on the node.
Administrators can enable NvFractions during KAI Scheduler installation with a Helm flag, and workloads declare fractional GPU requirements using annotations such as absolute memory sizes, portion-based fractions, optional burst limits, and compute mode selection.
Next Steps
Explore the
GPU Fractioning Operator repository
for installation and configuration instructions.
Review the
admin guide
and
user guide
for the three GPU sharing mechanisms.
Join the
Slack channel
or
bi-weekly community meetings
to ask questions and contribute.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU. Giving each one an entire device can leave capacity idle; sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the infrastructure they already have.
NVIDIA GPUs already support several approaches to sharing. Multi-instance GPU (MIG) splits a GPU into hardware-isolated instances that are transparent to the application, time-slicing lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement, and
Multi-Process Service
(MPS) lets them run concurrently in separate address spaces (sm-sharing).
CUDA 13.4 now enforces a memory boundary that is transparent to the application with a new time-sharing mode, alongside the compute sharing mode (sm-sharing) that already existed in MPS.
Here is what the
CUDA release
brings:
An exact memory amount:
A workload asks for a memory size and CUDA holds it there. An allocation above that size fails, just as it would on a smaller GPU.
A range:
A workload gets a guaranteed minimum plus a maximum it can grow into when memory is free.
A compute mode:
Each workload can choose to use its compute in an sm-sharing mode rather than using the default time-sharing mode.
A transparent memory limit:
Each workload sees only a fraction of the GPU memory.
The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes
CUDA provides the memory enforcement capability, but a Kubernetes cluster can’t use it on its own. On every GPU node, something has to:
Run and supervise the daemons that these features depend on
Apply each Pod container’s memory limits and compute mode before the process starts
Report what each fraction actually uses, rather than what the whole GPU uses
This work belongs on the node, independent of whichever scheduler placed the workload.
GPU fractioning: An open-source Kubernetes operator
A new open-source Kubernetes operator,
gpu-fractioning
, is  hosted under the
KAI Scheduler
organization on GitHub. It runs next to the
NVIDIA GPU Operator,
which provides the driver and the container runtime setup.
GPU Fractioning Operator handles three jobs:
It sets up and runs MPS on every GPU node.
It applies each workload’s memory limits and compute mode.
It measures memory and compute use per fraction rather than per GPU.
How schedulers pass GPU allocations to the operator
The developers write the resource and mode annotations in the pod YAML. Then the scheduler selects the GPUs for a workload and records its memory allocation and compute-sharing mode in per-container Pod annotations. GPU Fractioning Operator reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to apply the workload’s memory limits and compute mode:
Annotation
Meaning
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.request
Guaranteed GPU memory
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.limit
Maximum the container may grow into
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode
time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing
nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpus.devices
Which GPUs the container was assigned
Table 1: Per-container Pod annotations that GPU Fractioning Operator reads to enforce a GPU fraction
Any Kubernetes scheduler that can write these annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA. The scheduler still has its own job: choosing a GPU with enough free memory and never mixing compute modes on one GPU.
Using GPU Fractioning with KAI Scheduler
KAI Scheduler is the first scheduler integrated with
gpu-fractioning
. Starting with v0.18.0, KAI Scheduler has a GPU-sharing mode called
NvFractions
. KAI Scheduler picks which slice of which GPU each workload gets and writes the annotations (see Table 1, above), and
gpu-fractioning
enforces them on the node.
KAI Scheduler’s other sharing modes stay available, and administrators choose one per cluster. It can be enabled when KAI is installed:
helm upgrade -i kai-scheduler oci://ghcr.io/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler \
-n kai-scheduler --create-namespace \
--set global.nvFractions.set=true
This also installs
gpu-fractioning
as a dependency. From then on, you describe a fractional workload with Pod annotations.
There are four important annotations that answer four questions:
1. How much memory is needed
2. How far the workload may grow
3. How compute is shared
4. How many GPUs it spans
How much memory: The request
There are two ways to request memory:
1. As an absolute size:
Use the per-container NVIDIA annotation and standard Kubernetes units:
The container name (
app
) is part of the key, so it always targets the right container.
2. As a portion of a GPU by using KAI Scheduler’s existing annotation:
gpu-fraction: "0.5"
How far it may grow: The limit
This ability is new in KAI Scheduler. A workload can declare a guaranteed minimum (the request) and a maximum it may burst into when memory is free. Which limit annotation you use depends on how you wrote the request:
Request Type
Annotation
Example
Absolute Size
nvidia.com/container.<c>.gpu-memory.limit
“80Gi”
A Portion
kai.scheduler/container.<c>.gpu-memory.portion.limit
“0.8”
Table 2
:
Which limit annotation to use for each type of memory request
The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for. A portion limit must be greater than the
gpu-fraction
and less than 1.
How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing
Figure 1. Time-slicing divides the GPU’s time. SM-sharing divides its streaming multiprocessors (sm)
Compute can now be divided. Call n the number of workloads sharing a GPU: either way each gets roughly 1/n of the compute, and what differs is whether they take turns or run together.
Time-slicing is serial:
Workloads take turns on the whole GPU, and when every one of them uses its full slice each gets about 1/n of the time. Time left unused by one workload is shared equally between the others. This is the default. Each workload runs in its own error domain, i.e. full error isolation.
SM-sharing is parallel:
The GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs) are split between workloads and all run at once, continuously. Nothing is carved out in advance. The GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs as workloads need them. When every workload is busy the split settles at roughly 1/n; when one goes quiet its SMs go to the others, and a single active workload can use them all. In this mode, workloads share a single error domain.
Compute mode is now explicit and can be set per container:
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing"   # or "time-slicing"
A shared GPU runs one compute mode at a time, so KAI Scheduler never places a time-slicing workload and an sm-sharing workload on the same GPU. KAI Scheduler tracks this per GPU, not per node, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs.
How many GPUs are utilized
To get fractional capacity on several devices, add:
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"
The request applies to each device. A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs.
Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning
An absolute size with room to burst on four GPUs with SM-sharing:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: inference
labels:
kai.scheduler/queue: default-queue
annotations:
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.request: "40Gi"
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.limit: "60Gi"       # optional
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # optional, default time-slicing
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"                           # optional, default 1
spec:
schedulerName: kai-scheduler
containers:
- name: app
image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-base-ubuntu24.04
This is an inference server split across four GPUs that needs a guaranteed 40Gi on each GPU, can use up to 60Gi when neighbors are idle, and runs alongside other workloads instead of waiting its turn. SM-sharing puts the workloads in one error domain, so use it for workloads you trust to run together.
Half a GPU that may grow to 80% on two GPUs with time slicing (default):
metadata:
annotations:
gpu-fraction: "0.5"
gpu-fraction.limit: "0.8"  # optional
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "time-slicing"    # optional
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "2"                                # optional
spec:
schedulerName: kai-scheduler
containers:
- name: app
This is an example for a development or batch job, such as notebooks or small fine-tuning runs, that need a guaranteed half of each of two GPUs and can grow to 80% when memory is free. Time-slicing gives each workload its own error domain, so a crash in one job doesn’t affect its neighbors. Running
nvidia-smi
in the container should show two GPUs, each with this workload’s fractional memory share.
Getting started
KAI Scheduler and the
GPU Fractioning
Operator are both on GitHub under
the KAI Scheduler organization
, with installation and configuration instructions for all three sharing mechanisms (See
admin
and
user
guides). Join
the Slack channel
or
bi-weekly community meetings
to ask your questions and contribute.
For more information about CUDA 13.4,
refer to the announcement.
You can also get involved during
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026
in Salt Lake City, Utah
, Nov. 9-12.

Export to a self-managed BigQuery project
Supported in:
Google SecOps
Google Security Operations lets you export Unified Data Model (UDM) data to a self-managed project
that you own and manage. You can link your own Google Cloud project to your
Google SecOps instance and independently manage IAM
permissions with no dependency on Google-managed settings. You can also enable and
configure the
Bring Your Own BigQuery
(BYOBQ) feature by selecting
SIEM Settings
>
Data Export
.
Note:
Enabling BYOBQ on your
Bring your own project
(BYOP) project
may incur additional storage and compute costs.
Note:
BYOBQ is not available for Google SecOps
Enterprise Plus customers.
Google SecOps exports the following categories of data to your
BigQuery project:
udm_events
: log data normalized into the UDM schema.
udm_events_aggregates
: aggregated data that is summarized by each hour of normalized
events.
entity_graph
: There are three dimensions (contextual data, derived data, and global
context) to the entity graph. All of contextual data and derived data,
as well as part of global context data is data written and stored as
UDM.
rule_detections
: detections that are returned by rules run in Google SecOps.
ioc_matches
: IOC matches that are found against UDM events.
ingestion_metrics
: metrics related to the ingestion and normalization pipeline (exported by default).
udm_enum_value_to_name_mapping
: maps enum values to UDM field names (exported by default).
entity_enum_value_to_name_mapping
: maps enum values to entity field names (exported by default).
Retention period
If you're an existing customer, the retention period you set defines how long the
exported data for your BigQuery stays in your Google-managed project.
The retention period begins from the date of the earliest exported record. You can
configure a separate retention period for each data source, up to a maximum that
matches the default log retention period in Google SecOps.
If no retention period is specified, the default behavior is to keep exporting
data without any cleanup or purging, to limit the retention period.
In this case, you can set the retention period to
Unlimited
:
Click
SIEM Settings
>
Data Export
.
In the
Retention Period
column of the
Data Export
table, select
Unlimited
from the list for the relevant data type.
You can then set up an
object lifecycle rule
in your Google Cloud storage bucket to delete objects as needed.
Data migration for existing customers
If you're an existing customer, your data from the existing Google-managed
project isn't migrated to the self-managed project. Because data isn't migrated, your data is
located in two separate projects. To query the data across a time range that
includes the self-managed project activation date, you need to complete one of
the following actions:
Use a single query that joins data across both projects.
Run two separate queries on the respective projects, one for data before
the self-managed project activation date and one for data after.
When the retention period for your Google-managed project expires, that data
is deleted. You can only query data that is within your Google Cloud
project after that point.
Permissions required to export data
To access your BigQuery data, run your queries within BigQuery
itself. Assign the following IAM roles to any user who needs access:
BigQuery Data Viewer
(
roles/bigquery.dataViewer
)
BigQuery Job User
(
roles/bigquery.jobUser
)
Storage Object Viewer
(
roles/storage.objectViewer
)
You can also assign roles at the dataset level. For more information, see
BigQuery IAM roles and permissions
.
Initiate BigQuery data export to your self-managed project
Create a Google Cloud project where you want your data to be exported.
For more information, see
Configure a Google Cloud project for Google SecOps
.
Note:
The self-managed project must be linked to the Google SecOps instance.
Once this capability is enabled, you can't revert to a Google-managed project.
Link your self-managed project to your Google SecOps instance
to establish a connection between Google SecOps and your self-managed
project. For more information, see
Link Google Security Operations to Google Cloud services
.
You can also enable and configure the
Bring Your Own BigQuery
(BYOBQ) feature
by selecting
SIEM Settings
>
Data Export
.
To validate that the data is exported to your self-managed project, check the
tables under the
datalake
dataset in BigQuery.
You can write ad-hoc queries against Google SecOps data stored
in BigQuery tables. You can also create more advanced analytics using
other third-party tools that integrate with BigQuery.
All the resources created in the your self-managed Google Cloud project to enable
exports, including Cloud Storage bucket and BigQuery tables, are in the same
region as Google SecOps.
If you get an error like
Unrecognized name: <field_name> at [<some_number>:<some_number>]
when querying BigQuery, it means the field you're trying to access isn't
in your dataset and because your schema is dynamically generated
during the export process.
For more information about Google SecOps data in BigQuery,
see
Google SecOps data in BigQuery
.
Related API methods
Use the API methods described in the following topics to access export configurations
and manage how your data is sent to BigQuery:
BigQueryExport
REST Resource: projects.locations.instances.bigQueryExport

items.title: Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents See Google A2Ui in action! Learn how to natively render agentic UIs across Langchain, AWS Strands, Microsoft agents, and Goog
items.content:
Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
- Google Developers Blog
Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
OCT. 29, 2026
Google A2UI Team
Atai Barkai
CEO at CopilotKit
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Agent-User Interactions are now evolving from text exchanges to rich UIs. Until recently, most conversations looked like this:
User:
"Find me a holiday package to Bali in March."
Agent:
(six packages in prose, each with dates, hotel, flights, price)
User:
"The five-night one with breakfast."
Agent:
"Here's the link. You can book it on the operator's site."
Agents could plan the trip, but everything came back as walls of text. They had no standard way to render a selectable list of packages, a map of the destinations, or a date picker to carry you through the rest of the booking, inside the conversation itself.
Generative UI is the layer that lets agents build interfaces at runtime, shaped by what each request needs - giving users a rich, interactive experience. Implementing that takes two pieces: a way to describe the UI and an agentic stack that connects your agent to your application and renders that UI.
A2UI (Agent-to-UI)
is Google's framework-agnostic open standard for Generative UI. The agent describes an interface as data, and your application draws it with the components you already have. It's transport-agnostic by design.
CopilotKit
provides the agent-integration stack to integrate with agent frameworks like “LangChain”, “AWS Strands”, “Google ADK”, etc. for building user-facing agentic apps. It provides a toolkit for building rich applications with A2UI protocol, including the chat surface, runtime, and leverages A2UI renderer, across React and Angular. CopilotKit also provides custom A2UI renderers for Vue and Slack.
What is A2UI?
Generative UI covers a spectrum of approaches, from using predefined higher order components, to enabling your AI agent to have the flexibility to decide how to build the UI.
At the controlled end, you build each component ahead of time, and the agent picks which one to render and with what data. It's brand-safe but it does not allow for deep customization and personalization based on the user’s intent. At the open end, the agent returns a raw UI program written in HTML, Javascript and/or Dart that renders inside a sandboxed iframe. That covers anything you did not plan for, at the cost of a surface that drifts from your design system and executes code a model wrote.
A2UI
works through the entire spectrum. It participates in
controlled generation with decision models
like Typesafe’s Jev and also open-ended code generation that may output A2UI JSON messages. The declarative mode, where agents assemble pre-declared components and functions, is the most popular. A2UI is the framework-agnostic standard for declaring UI intent, so local or remote agents can generate your UI from your existing component catalog using a common language.
Security first.
A2UI is a declarative data format rather than executable code. The client keeps a catalog of trusted components, so anything the agent invents outside that set is caught before it reaches the screen.
LLM-friendly and streaming.
The payload is a flat list of small JSON messages that reference each other by ID, so the agent emits it incrementally and the client renders components as they arrive.
Framework-agnostic and portable.
The same response renders through
React, Lit, Angular, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose (Android) or Flutter
(multi-platform), and through
community renderers
for Vue, or even the terminal.
Frontend developers can now ship the building blocks once, and the agent composes them for each request.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
The
Basic Catalog
ships 18 general-purpose primitives across layout, display, input, and containers. The agent can compose entirely different interfaces from the same 18 primitives, depending on what the request needs.
The Basic Catalog is deliberately sparse, so most production apps
define their own custom catalog
. A custom component can be anything your frontend already renders, including a live map the agent fills with coordinates while your renderer draws the route.
How A2UI and CopilotKit work together
CopilotKit is built on
AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol)
, which supports A2UI payload and provides Agent SDKs across many agentic backends.
Your agent emits A2UI operations. AG-UI carries them to the client as typed events. When the user takes any action, the values are sent back along the same stream.
A2UI works with any AG-UI compatible agent.
Frameworks like Google ADK, LangChain, Mastra and Strands are all AG-UI compatible, so the setup is identical whichever one your agent runs on.
Setting up A2UI in your app
Setup comes down to two things: connecting your agent to CopilotKit, and defining which components the agent is allowed to use.
Using Google ADK as the example, the
ag_ui_adk
package wraps any ADK agent and serves it as an AG-UI endpoint on FastAPI:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from ag_ui_adk import ADKAgent, add_adk_fastapi_endpoint
root_agent = LlmAgent(
name="flight_agent",
model="gemini-3.8-flash",
instruction="Help users find and book flights. Call generate_a2ui to show results.",
)
adk_agent = ADKAgent(
adk_agent=root_agent,
app_name="flights",
user_id="demo_user",
use_in_memory_services=True,
)
app = FastAPI()
add_adk_fastapi_endpoint(app, adk_agent, path="/")
Python
Copied
On the app side, you register that endpoint with the CopilotKit runtime at
/api/copilotkit
. It's a few lines of standard setup, covered in the
Google ADK quickstart
, and it needs nothing A2UI-specific.
A2UI itself turns on from the client, where your components already are. Define what the agent is allowed to draw, map each definition to a renderer, and pass the catalog to the CopilotKit provider.
import { CopilotKit, CopilotChat } from '@copilotkit/react-core/v2';
import {
createCatalog,
type CatalogDefinitions,
type CatalogRenderers,
} from '@copilotkit/a2ui-renderer';
import { z } from 'zod';
const catalogDefinitions = {
FlightCard: {
description: 'A flight result with airline, times, and stops.',
props: z.object({
airline: z.string(),
departs: z.string(),
arrives: z.string(),
stops: z.number(),
}),
},
} satisfies CatalogDefinitions;
const catalogRenderers = {
FlightCard: MyFlightCard, // your React component
} satisfies CatalogRenderers<typeof catalogDefinitions>;
const catalog = createCatalog(catalogDefinitions, catalogRenderers, {
catalogId: 'flight-catalog',
includeBasicCatalog: true,
});
<CopilotKit runtimeUrl="/api/copilotkit" a2ui={{ catalog }}>
<CopilotChat />
</CopilotKit>
JavaScript
Copied
The
description
goes into the agent's prompt, so the model knows when to reach for
FlightCard
instead of a generic card. The Zod schema validates the props it sends back.
The A2UI configuration can be set up ahead of time on the server, or it can be created dynamically, shipped from the client to the server with the request. The ADK code above used dynamic configuration which is why it used generate_a2ui without defining it. The
docs
cover both approaches.
That’s the CopilotKit path. You can also consume the event stream directly with
@ag-ui/client
and hand the A2UI operations to any compliant renderer:
@a2ui/react
, or the Flutter, Lit, or Angular equivalent.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Building bi-directional A2UI surfaces
Most agent-generated UI is one-shot. The agent draws something, you read it, and it goes stale the moment anything changes.
A2UI surfaces are bi-directional and the components are reactive
, which makes multi-step flows possible. Any action the user takes on the interface (picking dates, choosing a flight, entering passenger details) travels back along the same stream, and the agent re-emits the surface from there using those values.
Here is a high-level architecture example of an end-to-end booking flow, with an AG-UI agent on Cloud Run streaming A2UI surfaces to a CopilotKit frontend.
Two things make the round trip work: inputs bound to a data path, and a button carrying an action that names which paths to send back.
{ "id": "cabin", "component": "ChoicePicker", "variant": "mutuallyExclusive",
"options": [ { "label": "Economy", "value": "eco" },
{ "label": "Business", "value": "biz" } ],
"value": { "path": "/booking/cabin" } },
{ "id": "confirm", "component": "Button", "child": "confirm_label",
"action": { "event": { "name": "confirmBooking",
"context": { "cabin": { "path": "/booking/cabin" },
"email": { "path": "/booking/email" } } } } }
JSON
Copied
Validation runs on the client, so a bad email shows an error inline without a model call. Nothing reaches the agent until the button fires.
Then the client sends the bound values, and the agent re-emits against the same
surfaceId
. That is how the whole flow lives on one surface: flight search, results, passenger details, and confirmation.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Benefits of running A2UI over AG-UI
Every AG-UI integration inherets these benefits, so you don't have to build them yourself:
Minimal server-side setup:
the catalog reaches the agent on setup, so registering it on the client is all it takes.
Generation in a dedicated sub-agent:
the catalog and protocol rules stay out of your main agent's context window, and the surface streams to the client as the sub-agent produces it.
Self-healing output:
invalid generations are caught and the specific errors go back for a correction, so nothing broken reaches the screen.
Graceful failure:
when retries are exhausted, the surface resolves to a short message and the conversation continues instead of dying in an error state.
Get Started
Create a complete A2UI + CopilotKit application. This creates a starter A2UI application with Copilotkit Agent integration.
npx copilotkit@latest create --name my-app --framework a2ui
Shell
Copied
The
CopilotKit Dojo
has runnable A2UI demos: fixed server-side schema, dynamic schema against a custom catalog, and an error-recovery example where an invalid first render heals into a valid one.
A2UI Composer
CopilotKit A2UI Docs
Use A2UI with Any Agent Framework & Harness
Explore how to build Generative UI Agents with
CopilotKit
, or dive into
A2UI documentation
to learn how to integrate A2UI with any framework of your choice.

items.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous test
items.content:
Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
- Google Developers Blog
Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
OCT. 28, 2026
Pier Paolo Ippolito
Product Manager
Elia Secchi
Solutions Specialist
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
A live walkthrough of the Agents CLI eval loop, from a first run to regression tracking, model-backend experiments, and automated alerting
Introduction
Building an agent that works on a demo is a different problem from building an agent that stays working across model upgrades, tool changes, and new conversation shapes. The first takes a weekend; the second takes a loop. A team writes test cases, runs them, grades them, reads what failed, changes the agent, and runs the cases again. If the score goes up, the change was good. If it goes down, revert. Over weeks of this, the agent inches toward the ceiling of what the model, tools, and prompt can do together. The quality-engineering name for this is hill-climbing.
The Agents CLI eval namespace was built around this loop. The commands are small and framework-agnostic: eval generate runs the agent against a dataset of cases, eval grade scores the generated traces, eval compare diffs two run results side by side, eval analyze clusters failures into themes, and eval optimize runs an automated hill-climbing pass on the agent's prompt.
Below: baseline → regression → model swap → scheduling and alerting.
Setup
The scaffold used throughout is the LangChain template that ships with Agents CLI v1.8.0. The setup is a single command:
agents-cli create my-agent \
--agent google/agents-cli/extensions/langchain/template@v1.8.0 \
-d cloud_run
cd my-agent && agents-cli install
Plain text
Copied
The scaffold ships with an eval dataset at
tests/eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json,
a config at
tests/eval/eval_config.yaml
, and a custom LLM-as-judge metric at
tests/eval/response_quality.py
. The config declares the metric to run:
# tests/eval/eval_config.yaml
metrics_to_run:
- custom_response_quality
custom_metrics:
- name: custom_response_quality
custom_function_file: response_quality.py
Plain text
Copied
The metric grades each response on a 1-to-5 scale for accuracy, relevance, and clarity, using
gemini-3.8-flash
as the judge. The default dataset has a single trivial case, which is not enough for a hill-climb. The first thing we do is expand it to four cases that probe different behaviors:
{
"eval_cases": [
{"name": "greeting",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "hello"}]}}]}]}},
{"name": "sf_weather",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "What is the weather in San Francisco?"}]}}]}]}},
{"name": "rome_weather",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "How is the weather in Rome today?"}]}}]}]}},
{"name": "off_topic",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "Who won the 2024 World Series?"}]}}]}]}}
]
}
Plain text
Copied
Four cases: a greeting, a weather question the mock tool handles with the hardcoded foggy response, a weather question for a city the tool defaults on, and an off-topic question that the agent has to decide how to handle. This is a small dataset by design; the hill-climbing loop pays off when the dataset is small enough to run on every change.
Step 1: Running the First Eval
With the dataset in place, we
run eval generate
to drive the agent against each case, then
eval grade
to score the resulting traces:
agents-cli eval generate --dataset tests/eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json \
-o tests/eval/output/
agents-cli eval grade --traces tests/eval/output/eval_dataset_*.json \
--config tests/eval/eval_config.yaml
Plain text
Copied
The baseline run produces:
Evaluation Summary
custom_response_quality:
num_cases_total: 4
num_cases_valid: 4
num_cases_error: 0
mean_score: 4.0000
stdev_score: 1.4142
Saved full results to artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_224516.json
Saved HTML results to artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_224516.html
Plain text
Copied
Mean 4.0 out of 5 across four cases, with a standard deviation of 1.41. That stdev tells us immediately that the cases are not scoring uniformly, which is a healthier starting point than a flat 5.0 across the board. A flat 5.0 either means the agent is perfect (unlikely) or the dataset is too easy to show variation. 4.0 with real spread is a hill to climb.
Step 2: Making a Change and Re-Running
To demonstrate the loop, we introduce a realistic regression. A developer working across several agent projects accidentally pastes the wrong system prompt into our weather agent: a chef persona meant for a different codebase. In
app/agent.py
:
# Before
root_agent: CompiledStateGraph = create_agent(
model=llm, tools=[get_weather], system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant"
)
# After
root_agent: CompiledStateGraph = create_agent(
model=llm, tools=[get_weather],
system_prompt=(
"You are a professional chef. Help users with recipes, cooking "
"techniques, and ingredient substitutions. Always suggest a recipe "
"at the end of every response."
),
)
Plain text
Copied
The change compiles, the agent still runs, and nothing in the pre-eval pipeline (lint, unit tests, type checks) catches it. Re-running the same eval generate plus eval grade sequence produces:
Evaluation Summary
custom_response_quality:
num_cases_total: 4
num_cases_valid: 4
num_cases_error: 0
mean_score: 2.7500
stdev_score: 0.9574
Saved full results to artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_225158.json
JSON
Copied
Mean 2.75, down from 4.0. The judge agrees with our intuition that a chef persona on a weather agent is a worse product than a general-purpose helpful assistant. The stdev also tightened from 1.41 to 0.96, consistent with the chef prompt pushing most cases toward the same mediocre range.
A 1.25-point drop on a 1-to-5 scale is substantial, and the kind of regression that can slip through code review when the diff looks small ("one string literal changed"). The loop surfaced the change at all, with a specific number attached to it, before the agent reached production.
Step 3: Comparing Two Runs
Mean scores are a start; the per-case diff is where the hill-climb happens. eval compare reads two result files and produces a structured JSON diff:
agents-cli eval compare \
artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_224516.json \
artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_225158.json
JSON
Copied
The output lists which keys changed and which stayed the same:
{
"baseline_keys": ["agent_info", "eval_case_results", "evaluation_dataset",
"metadata", "summary_metrics", "win_rates"],
"candidate_keys": ["agent_info", "eval_case_results", "evaluation_dataset",
"metadata", "summary_metrics", "win_rates"],
"changed_keys": ["eval_case_results", "metadata.creation_timestamp"],
"unchanged_keys": ["agent_info", "evaluation_dataset", "metadata",
"summary_metrics", "win_rates"],
"differences": { ... per-case score diffs ... }
}
JSON
Copied
The
differences
object has the full per-case breakdown with the baseline and candidate values side by side. For a hill-climbing workflow, we typically pipe the output through
jq
or a small Python script to extract the signal; the raw JSON is the complete evidence.
Step 4: Reading the Per-Case Scores
Walking the two result files and lining up the scores per case shows where the regression landed:
case                  baseline → candidate   what the chef prompt did
greeting              5.0 → 4.0  ↓          launched into an unsolicited recipe pitch after "hello"
sf_weather            4.0 → 2.0  ↓          ignored the weather tool, hallucinated conditions
rome_weather          2.0 → 2.0  ·          already hallucinated at baseline; chef persona did not make it worse
off_topic             5.0 → 3.0  ↓          answered the Dodgers question but tacked on a recipe
Plain text
Copied
Three cases dropped, one held. The most important of the three is
sf_weather
: the chef persona pulled the model's attention away from the registered
get_weather
tool, so the agent stopped calling it and started making up weather values. Unit tests can't catch this: the code runs, the tool is still registered, but the model's behavior around it has shifted. Only an end-to-end eval that scores the response in context surfaces this.
The mean drop by itself (−1.25) is a clear signal, but the per-case breakdown is what tells the developer where to look. A one-line system-prompt change propagated through three different cases in three different ways: greeting lost a point on tone,
sf_weather
lost two on tool usage,
off_topic
lost two on scope creep.
Step 5: Swapping the Model Backend
A common hill-climbing question is whether a cheaper or faster model would do the job acceptably. For the LangChain template, the model is defined in
app/agent.py
:
LLM = "gemini-3.8-flash"
llm = ChatGoogleGenerativeAI(model=LLM, temperature=0)
Plain text
Copied
We swap
gemini-3.8-flash
for
gemini-2.5-flash
(restoring the helpful system prompt first), re-run
eval generate
plus
eval grade
, and compare the two result files. The mean drops from 4.00 to 2.75, the same magnitude as the chef-prompt regression, but the per-case breakdown tells a completely different story:
case                  3.8-flash → 2.5-flash
greeting              5.0 → 5.0  ·
sf_weather            4.0 → 3.0  ↓
rome_weather          2.0 → 2.0  ·
off_topic             5.0 → 1.0  ↓↓
Plain text
Copied
The cheaper model matched 3.8-flash exactly on the greeting and rome_weather cases and lost a point on sf_weather (slightly less polished phrasing). The whole visible drop traces to
off_topic
, where the cheaper model refused with a hedge about the event "not having happened yet" (a training-cutoff artifact), and the judge marked it harshly.
The lesson is that the summary number is misleading. Look only at the mean and you'd call
gemini-2.5-flash
as bad as the chef prompt. Look at the per-case breakdown and you'd call it a reasonable swap for most of the agent's workload, with one case (handling out-of-scope questions about recent events) exposing a real limitation. If the production distribution of user questions matches the first three cases more than the fourth, the swap is worth considering. If
off_topic
-style questions are common, it is not.
Two caveats on this experiment. First, model swaps interact with the prompt: a prompt tuned for a stronger model often leaks capability when ported to a weaker one, so the right comparison is "weaker model with a prompt tuned for it" versus "stronger model with its own tuned prompt." Second, the Vertex AI Eval Service calls a judge model to grade the traces, and the judge is held constant across the comparison. Changing the judge is a different experiment and should be done separately.
Step 6: Scheduling the Loop
Agents CLI does not ship a scheduler, but the
eval
commands are designed to drop into standard infrastructure. The pattern we can use here is a cron job or Cloud Scheduler trigger that runs
eval generate
plus
eval grade
on a cadence and writes the results to a persistent location:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/scheduled_eval.sh — invoked nightly by cron or Cloud Scheduler
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d)
OUT=artifacts/scheduled_runs/$DATE
mkdir -p $OUT
agents-cli eval generate --dataset tests/eval/datasets/regression.json -o $OUT/
agents-cli eval grade --traces $OUT/eval_dataset_*.json \
--config tests/eval/eval_config.yaml \
--output $OUT/
Plain text
Copied
A nightly run against a stable regression dataset catches drift from model updates, data changes in the agent's tools, and dependencies that shift under the agent's feet. For a production agent, the scheduled run also captures the model vendor's quiet upgrades, which can move the agent's behavior without any change on our side. The dataset for the scheduled run is typically larger than the one used in the inner loop (dozens to hundreds of cases rather than a few), since it only runs once a day.
Step 7: Alerting on Score Drops
The scheduled run produces a result file every day, but a file nobody looks at is not an alert. The pattern here can be a wrapper script that compares each new run's mean against a baseline (the previous run, or a committed known-good) and exits non-zero when the drop exceeds a threshold. The non-zero exit is what triggers the alert from the surrounding scheduler.
Here is an example:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Exit non-zero if an eval result dips below baseline by more than --threshold."""

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster
items.content:
Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
- Google Developers Blog
Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
OCT. 28, 2026
Google AI Edge Team
Android ML Team
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
LiteRT in Google Play services is Android's on-device inference runtime for custom models, handling more than a trillion inferences a day across billions of devices. Today, it gets its
biggest upgrade yet:
GPU inference that runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy GPU delegate
, powered by
ML Drift
and available through the new
CompiledModel API
, LiteRT’s modern successor to the legacy Interpreter API.
Until now, taking advantage of this faster GPU stack required bundling LiteRT in your app.
In our testing, apps that switched to LiteRT in Google Play services are about 8 MB smaller
,
making them faster to download and lighter on users' devices
, because the runtime, including the GPU accelerator, ships once with Play services rather than inside every app. More than 100K Android apps bundle their own copy of LiteRT or TensorFlow Lite today, so the savings add up quickly as apps switch.
If your Android app runs custom ML models on CPU or GPU, we encourage you to switch to LiteRT in Google Play services.
You can see it in action in the
Google AI Edge Gallery
app, where the Scrapbook feature's image segmentation runs on LiteRT in Google Play services.
Why use LiteRT in Google Play services
Developers that adopt LiteRT in Google Play Services enjoy immediate benefits:
Smaller apps, more free storage
: As no ML runtime is bundled into your APK, your app is smaller and faster to download. In addition, as apps share one runtime, the storage and memory savings grow with each app that switches.
Automatic updates
: performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches arrive through Play services in staged rollouts that catch device-specific issues early, without you having to ship an app update.
More places to run
: LiteRT in Play services runs on phones back to Android 7 (API level 24), and now also on Wear OS 4+ and Android Automotive OS (Android 11+).
Tested at scale
: ML Kit's Vision and Text APIs, like
Subject Segmentation
and
Document Scanner
, are already powered by LiteRT in Google Play services at scale across billions of Android devices. By adopting LiteRT in Google Play Services you are using the same, battle-tested infrastructure in your own app.
CompiledModel API
LiteRT is the evolution of TensorFlow Lite. It keeps the same .tflite model format you rely on and adds the CompiledModel API, which makes acceleration across fragmented hardware reliable:
Simpler
: one workflow for CPU and GPU acceleration instead of a different delegate and setup path for each accelerator. LiteRT uses OpenCL where available and OpenGL otherwise. If you request both GPU and CPU, it falls back to CPU on devices without a usable GPU.
Faster
: powered by ML Drift, LiteRT's latest, open-source GPU engine already used by Google apps on millions of devices daily. GPU inference runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy TensorFlow Lite GPU delegate.
Portable
: cross-platform support, so the same
.tflite
model runs on Android, iOS, desktop, and web.
Flexible
: the legacy Interpreter API is still supported on CPU, so you can migrate in phases.
Getting started and upgrading
Whether you're starting fresh or switching from bundled LiteRT, using LiteRT in Google Play services takes a
few lines of code
:
Add
com.google.android.gms:play-services-litert:17.0.0
(or a later version). If you bundle LiteRT today, remove the
litert
dependency.
Get the
LiteRT
environment from Play services:
val liteRtEnvironment =
LiteRt.initialize(
context,
LiteRtDsl.initializationOptions { setEnableGpu(true) }
).await()
Kotlin
Copied
Pass the LiteRT
environment
in when you create your
CompiledModel
. The rest of your code stays the same.
If you're already using the legacy Interpreter API in Google Play services
, your Interpreter code keeps working on CPU when you switch to play-services-litert. To run on the GPU, move to the CompiledModel API.
Let your coding agent do the work.
In Agent Mode, the new LiteRT skill for Android Studio automates the move to LiteRT in Google Play services and the CompiledModel API. Ask it to “migrate my TFLite code to CompiledModel,” or type
@litert-runtime
, and it switches your app to play-services-litert, rewrites your Interpreter calls, and sets up GPU acceleration with CPU fallback. It can also scaffold a new LiteRT app. Treat it as a strong first pass: review the diff, build, and compare outputs on a real device.
Get the skill on GitHub
.
Upgrading from legacy APIs?
The legacy GPU delegate and custom delegate APIs are deprecated in favor of CompiledModel GPU acceleration and the
Compiler Plugin
and
Dispatch
APIs, and NNAPI will be removed starting in 2027. Older SDKs now receive critical security fixes only. Apps you've already shipped keep working, but plan your move to the CompiledModel API now: code that uses deprecated APIs won't compile against the latest SDK, and staying on an older SDK can cause conflicts as your other dependencies move forward. See the
release notes
for details.
What's next
Looking ahead, LiteRT in Google Play services is our foundation for running your own task-specific models on Android, with CPU and GPU acceleration.
LiteRT will keep getting regular updates, including better GPU acceleration and wider model coverage.
NPU support in Play services is actively being worked on.
Ready to start
?
Read the
LiteRT in Google Play services docs
Try the
LiteRT skill for Android Studio
Try Scrapbook in the
Google AI Edge Gallery
app
Something stopping you from switching, or need help? Reach out on
GitHub Discussions
or
file an issue
.
We can't wait to see what you build.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

Beyond benchmarks, Mistral Large 4's coding capabilities are validated by human preference. In Surge Code's blind pairwise evaluations, Mistral Large 4 was preferred over leading open-weight models including GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated.

Built for the Defenders.
Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching.
Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. Crucially, Mistral Large 4 handles these legitimate defensive security tasks without unnecessary refusals.
Artificial Analysis - Cyber Index

Safety has improved alongside capability. Our model’s built-in guardrails distinguishes between defensive and malicious, offensive cybersecurity tasks. It retains strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, while achieving an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests, the highest we measure among open models.
